Rate: $16–$22/hour
Type: Hourly Contract, Remote
Schedule: Flexible
Location: Remote
Language Requirement: Native fluency in English & Odia

At Mercor, we believe the safest AI is the one that's already been attacked — by us. We are assembling a red team for this project — human data experts who probe AI models with adversarial inputs, surface vulnerabilities, and generate the red team data that makes AI safer.

Red team conversational AI models and agents: jailbreaks, prompt injections, misuse cases, bias exploitation, multi-turn manipulation
Generate high-quality human data: annotate failures, classify vulnerabilities, and flag systemic risks
Apply structure: follow taxonomies, benchmarks, and playbooks to keep testing consistent
Document reproducibly: produce reports, datasets, and attack cases customers can act on
Who You Are:
Strong judgment about language and content — can tell whether an AI response is accurate, complete, and appropriate
Rigorous — notices subtle errors, inconsistencies, and gaps others skim past
Structured — works to guidelines and quality standards consistently
Communicative — explains reasoning clearly to technical and non-technical audiences
Adaptable — thrives moving across projects, task types, and customers

Nice-to-Have Specialties:
Adversarial ML: jailbreak datasets, prompt injection, RLHF/DPO attacks, model extraction
Cybersecurity: penetration testing, exploit development, reverse engineering
Socio-technical risk: harassment/disinfo probing, abuse analysis, conversational AI testing
Creative probing: psychology, acting, writing for unconventional adversarial thinking

Logistics:
Independent contractor role
Fully remote, flexible schedule
Weekly payments via Stripe or Wise
Unable to support H1-B or STEM OPT candidates

Mathematical Modeling

Experience working in Linux or terminal-based environments.

Ability to independently implement, test, and validate computational algorithms.
Strong understanding of numerical stability, error analysis, mathematical assumptions, and reproducibility.

Experience designing tests that distinguish mathematically valid solutions from approximate or numerically unstable ones

Most organizations do not fail at AI because models are weak.
They fail because the decision loop is still lagging the network.
Plans improve in a dashboard. The physical chain has already moved.
That gap is where cost, risk, and false confidence accumulate.
Recent research in the International Journal of Production Research frames a sharper answer: agentic supply chain digital twins  -  A-SCDTs  -  that combine agentic AI, digital twins, and model-based optimization and simulation. Dmitry Ivanov's ICARUS lens is useful here: Interaction, Creativity, Adaptation, Reasoning, Ubiquity, and Synchronization. The last word is the operating principle. Without synchronization, AI mainly accelerates yesterday's assumptions.
Two public cases show what synchronized decisioning looks like in practice.
At Microsoft's cloud supply chain, planners work with generative-AI support that surfaces demand, inventory, open orders, and lane constraints, then runs optimization and explains why a fulfillment path was chosen. Scenario questions can add constraints on the fly  -  without waiting for a separate modeling cycle. The point is not a prettier forecast. It is a living conversation with a constrained plan that stays current enough to act on.
Ford's published digital-twin work pushes the same idea deeper into the network. Intracompany, Tier-1, and deep-tier layers differ in visibility. Agentic adapters connect twins, models, and enterprise systems so risk signals can trigger stress tests before a disruption becomes a shortage narrative. Time-to-survive versus time-to-recover stops being a slide and becomes a decision trigger.
The leadership implication is uncomfortable and useful.
Buying agents without owning the twin is like hiring faster analysts for stale books.
Director-level judgment asks different questions: Which decisions require human veto? Which data contracts keep models honest? Which stress tests must run before autonomy expands?
AI is not the strategy.
A synchronized decision system is.
Autonomy is earned only after the twin, the constraints, and the audit trail can keep pace with reality.

Hiring managers keep asking me what separates a production LM stack from a pile of prompt strings that break every model bump. stanfordnlp/dspy is the framework I open when the diligence question is whether the team programs the model with typed signatures, composable modules, and optimizers that teach prompts and weights, or still ships brittle prompt paste and calls the demo an agent platform ready for B2B customers.

~38.3k stars. ~3.4k forks. ~219 watchers. MIT. Live push on Sep 25 2026. Python. Homepage dspy.ai. Declarative Self-improving Python for classifiers, RAG, and agent loops.

The primitives that matter for B2B LM systems:
Signatures declare typed input to output contracts so the model return shape is owned.
Modules compose those signatures into real pipelines in Python, not in a chat window.
Optimizers (MIPRO, BootstrapFewShot, GEPA) teach prompts and weights instead of hoping the next rewrite sticks.

When I diligence an AI platform hire or an applied-LM product, this is the gate I write down:

Signatures over strings.
Optimizers over vibes.
Modular programs you can evaluate, not prompt museums you screenshot.

Prompt demos are cheap. Programmed LM systems are the bar for production B2B trust.

I have been watching the REST API landscape shift beneath our feet in 2026, and the most important change is not in the protocols themselves -- it is in how we measure and trust them.

The Uptrends API Reliability report shows a drop from 99.66% to 99.46% average uptime between Q1 2024 and Q1 2025. That 0.2% difference is a silent tax on every downstream service. For any system doing 10 million requests per day, that is 20,000 additional failures per quarter. The industry is normalizing fragility.

Errors now have a standard in RFC 9457. This is the quiet revolution. When every API returns a machine-readable problem detail object with a type URI, title, status, and detail, debugging shifts from reading logs to parsing structured contracts. I have seen teams cut incident resolution time by 40 percent simply by adopting this schema and teaching their clients to parse it. If your API still returns a generic 500 with a text message, you are building tech debt.

The non-obvious trend is how AI-generated clients are changing the design constraints. When an LLM generates your SDK code from an OpenAPI spec, it will strictly follow the spec. Any ambiguity, any undocumented edge case, any optional field that is really required -- these become hard failures. The era of "documentation as a suggestion" is over. Your API contract must be exact because the client will not interpret, it will execute.

Edge-deployed APIs are growing rapidly, and they force a different design philosophy. You cannot assume a round-trip to a central database. You need idempotency keys, conflict resolution strategies, and offline-first semantics baked into the contract. Serverless APIs dominate the deployment pattern, which means cold starts and connection pooling are architectural concerns, not operational ones.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am looking for teams that are building APIs with RFC 9457 error handling, strict OpenAPI contracts, and edge-ready idempotency patterns. If your organization is migrating from loosely-typed REST to robust, machine-readable API contracts, or if you are designing systems where AI agents will be primary consumers, I want to discuss how to design for reliability, debuggability, and cost efficiency from the start.

What is the one API design pattern you believe will define the next five years of backend development?

"AI is replacing developers."
I've heard this for two years. So I looked at the French numbers instead of repeating the headline.
INSEE, March 2026: IT employment in France fell 3% between end-2023 and end-2025.
Under-30s: −3.8 points.
30–54-year-olds: +1.4 points.
And the sector's output kept growing.
No mass layoffs. Companies simply stopped hiring juniors.
So on paper, seniors are safe.
Yet around me I see experienced engineers, some of them excellent, struggling to find a position or a contract. How do both things fit together?
Mostly, it's not AI.
There are fewer projects: IT cadre recruitment fell 21% in two years.
There are more seniors chasing the same missions.
And in large accounts, procurement often compares your daily rate before anyone understands your value.
AI does change something for seniors, but it doesn't replace them. It compresses teams. Where a project needed 6 developers, it may now need 2 plus good tooling. Knowing every corner of a framework is no longer a moat.
What stays scarce is understanding the real problem, choosing the right trade-off, and owning the result in production.
The catch is that this doesn't show on a CV. Everyone writes "problem solver." The market only sees it through concrete stories: the incident you diagnosed, the migration that didn't break, the decision that saved six months.
Being senior used to be enough. Now you have to make your value visible.
One question still bothers me.
Nobody is born a senior engineer. We all learned by writing the code that AI writes today.
If we stop hiring juniors now, where will Europe's engineers come from in 2032?
For those hiring right now: what actually makes a senior profile stand out for you today?

Balancing EU AI Act Compliance and US State Rules for Third Party Algorithmic Risk: Cont.

Third-party algorithms create liability even when the model is not yours
Third-party AI is now part of normal enterprise software. Hiring platforms score applicants. Fraud tools flag transactions. Customer service systems suggest responses. Insurance tools assess claims. Supply chain systems forecast disruption. Cybersecurity tools rank threats. Many of these systems include algorithms that the buyer cannot fully inspect. The vendor may cite intellectual property limits, security concerns, or technical complexity. Yet regulators and plaintiffs may still ask the enterprise a simple question.
**Why do a company rely on this system, and what does it do to manage the risk?
That question matters because liability does not always stop at the vendor. A company that deploys a third-party algorithm can still face legal exposure if the system harms workers, customers, patients, applicants, borrowers, or other affected people. Third-party algorithmic risk often appears in four ways.

Role confusion
The vendor may call itself a software provider. The enterprise may call itself a customer. Regulators may see both as part of the AI value chain. Under the EU AI Act, obligations can differ depending on whether an organization is a provider, deployer, importer, distributor, or product manufacturer. Those roles do not always follow contract labels. A company that substantially modifies a system or markets it under its own name may take on more responsibility than expected. In the United States, role labels also matter, but the focus often turns to control, use, notice, fairness, and consumer harm.

Opaque model behavior
A vendor may provide general accuracy claims but little detail about training data, model limits, drift, subgroup performance, or known failure modes. That creates a gap between what the enterprise can prove and what regulators may expect. If a system rejects qualified job applicants, flags legitimate customers as fraud risks, or denies access to a service, the enterprise needs more than a sales sheet. It needs evidence.

Data and privacy exposure
Third-party algorithms often process sensitive or regulated data. A model may use location data, biometric identifiers, health-related information, financial records, education data, employment history, or behavioral signals. Even if the vendor hosts the tool, the enterprise may remain responsible for lawful data use, retention, access controls, and individual rights.
Operational overreliance
A system described as “decision support” can become a de facto decision-maker if employees follow its outputs without meaningful review. That creates risk when the tool affects eligibility, pricing, ranking, scheduling, discipline, or access to benefits.

85% of American founders would start their company in the US again. In Germany, most wouldn't. That single gap tells you more about Europe's next decade than any funding headline…

Patrick Collison at Stripe just published a set of charts on European entrepreneurship and compute, and three of them, read together, hit pretty hard.

I say this as someone who chose to build in Europe, and still would. But the charts are sobering…

The first is AI payment volume. The US line climbs a wall while the EU line barely lifts off the floor - over three years it stays almost flat. That's not a gap between two markets, it's two different leagues. The stagnation is staggering. 

The second asks founders a simple question: would you incorporate in this country again? The US sits at 85% and Switzerland at 68%, and then the chart falls off a cliff for most of the EU.

The third rates dealing with government. Switzerland scores 8.2 and the US 7.6. Germany lands at 3.7 and Spain at 3.3, on a scale where 10 is easy.

I've lived both ends of this one. My previous company was in Germany, and that 3.7 felt exactly like a 3.7 every single week. My company today is Swiss-American: management in the US, engineering in Europe. For a founder, Switzerland versus Germany is night and day.

The hopeful reading is that Europe's problems look fixable - notaries, hiring and firing rules, slow permits, unclear regulation. I don't buy the timeline. Each of these has a constituency that likes it exactly the way it is, and that is a much harder thing to move than a bad law.

Take the notary. Someone reads every word of a 200-page contract out loud to you, then charges tens of thousands to confirm you understood the document you brought them in the first place. Ten pages in it could say you're selling your soul and nobody in the room would catch it.

Or take firing someone. It isn't a decision, it's a project, like building a house, only backwards, with a lawyer standing at every step.

None of this means Europe can't build great companies. It means the friction is a choice Europe keeps making, year after year. Switzerland chose differently, and it sits at the top of all three charts.

Walmart's culture turned its people into creators.

On LinkedIn, the same thing happened without a program

Riti Kumari is an SDE-III at Walmart Global Tech in Bengaluru with 291,305 followers and a 50K+ YouTube channel. She almost never posts about Walmart. She posts about how to get better at the job

"A year ago, hackathons were all about building CRUD apps. Today? The winning projects are AI-first products", 807 reactions. A post on why prompt engineering is the difference between good and bad AI output. A post on why "Location: Bangalore" means nothing until you know which Bangalore.

John Furner President and CEO of Walmart Inc., has 284,064 followers, and his best posts are about individual people

On the 25th anniversary of 9/11 he wrote about being a store manager in Jacksonville, North Carolina that morning, 1,072 reactions. A visit to the new Sam's Club in Tempe, where he met Renee Rangel, a cake decorator and the club's longest-tenured associate at 21 years, 915. A post on Walmart's truck drivers competing at the national championships, naming all six of them, 707

3) Half the top 10 is the leadership team, and they tag each other

Furner's truck driver post tags Donna Morris, Walmart's Chief People Officer (121,036 followers), and David Guggina, CEO of Walmart U.S.

Donna Morris posts from the floor too: the Sam's Club holiday meeting, a fashion pop-up in New York with lines out the door, a conversation with board memberCarla Harris

4) The engineering managers write about the craft

Abhishek Kumar is a Senior Engineering Manager, ex-Google and ex-founder, with 173,952 followers. One of his recent posts: "In a system design interview I can tell in 4 minutes if you built it or watched it"

Karun Thankachan a Senior Data Scientist with two ML patents and papers at ICLR, AAAI and NeurIPS, has 101,997

5) The recruiter who posts a role almost every day

Uzma Tabassum posts a specific open role at Walmart Global Tech on a near-daily cadence: a Network Engineer in Chennai, a Senior Full Stack Engineer in Bangalore, a QA Engineer, an SRE. Her announcement of a Java hiring drive in Chennai did 118

My takeaway: Walmart's biggest voices each have a lane. The engineer teaches, the CEO tells stories about associates, the executives tag each other, and the recruiters post constantly

A McKinsey report argued that 95% of a firm's value is produced by 5% of its workforce. An MIT professor spent years studying what that means for the other 95%. His answer: about 35% of the entire US workforce is now employed with no employer intention of retaining them.

Today on America's Work Force Union Podcast, MIT Sloan School of Management Professor Emeritus Paul Osterman discusses his book Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment, published by Harvard University Press in August 2026.

Key Discussion Points:

 • What a disposable worker is: Someone whom the employer, at the point of hiring or contracting, has no intention of retaining; four categories — lower-wage contractors such as building cleaners and security guards; high-earning contractors such as travel nurses; freelancers including gig workers and journalists; and marginal W-2 workers such as adjunct faculty and part-time service workers on no career track; together they represent approximately 35% of the US workforce per a nationally representative survey of 6,000 workers
 • Why companies do this: Benefit avoidance, including keeping workers under the 30-hour ACA threshold; wage suppression by forcing staffing companies to compete on labor cost; operational flexibility allowing instant termination without severance or HR process; and a McKinsey-documented corporate culture that treats the non-elite workforce as interchangeable
 • AI: Will accelerate the use of disposable workers because it creates organizational uncertainty that makes short-term, easily terminated arrangements more attractive; the long-term employment impact of AI is genuinely unknown, and anyone claiming certainty is making it up
 • The union answer: UNITE HERE hotel room attendants in Boston earn approximately $25 an hour with benefits under union contracts versus $13 to $14 an hour without benefits in non-union settings; union presence fundamentally changes the job even for contractor-classified workers; increasing union density is one of the most important structural interventions available; the evidence that workers are better off when a union is present is clear

PSA (public service announcement): If you are using AI at work to consolidate, synthesize, and/or summarize contents from multiple emails that originated from multiple platforms/systems... information in isolation that is safe on its own, can become at-risk when it is combined... and land you in an IT security protocol depending on the contents of the email and who it is sent to. 

Imagine you work in HR and are trying to gain efficiencies in onboarding consultants, FTEs, interns, strategic partners and/or vendors. 

Time is money and companies could look to AI to reduce training and onboarding costs that may be non-billable items in contracts between staffing agencies and their customers.

The thought has probably crossed someone's mind that it might be easier to just put all of the essential onboarding information into one email... and they may be thinking that this is an innovative and efficient time saver.  

So, let's say someone without a senior HR and/or compliance background has the idea to combine the contents from multiple emails into one. It could be a person who knows AI can be a time-savings hack, but maybe is not the most well-versed in data security and compliance. To this person, this use case could sound like a genius productivity hack.

If this is you or someone you know, listen up, it may seem harmless and it may be pretty common... but here's how it can go horribly wrong for you and the people involved.

Onboarding emails can involve sensitive information, system access credentials, multiple people on a CC list... and if you are not careful, a simple email could land your consultant in a Data Security protocol, off the job and at risk of termination... not to mention putting the HR professional, the resource manager, the hiring manager, the staffing agency and the company at risk.  

Imagine a scenario where the username and password are in two separate emails and an AI workflow combine it into one. On the CC: list are the hiring manager, the staffing agency and someone else identified as a line manager.

It gets sent on a Friday before a Monday start date... with instructions to wait 24 hours after first log-in to change the password. 

The moment it gets compiled, even before it is sent, the damage is done. The company and the new hire are immediately part of a High Risk, enterprise threat prevention system and triage tree (assuming your CISO is a good one).

The work that the consultant was there to do is at risk too. A team that needed a resource ASAP, who gets tied up in a compliance protocol, will likely blame the consultant and/or get frustrated and cut ties instead of looking in the mirror and owning up to the issue.    

If you are in need of an independent Human-first experience audit, backed with credibility and trust, we would love to help you in a safe and confidential, planned scenario setting so everyone involved knows it is a test of the emergency broadcast system (but without those annoying beeps).

Santanu Sarkar calls himself a "Headhunter!" and recruits for senior staff roles in India. His post for iOS and Android engineers on Uber's payments team drew 42 comments

3) The engineers build audiences on the industry, not the company

@Anmol A., a Software Engineer 2 with 140,232 LinkedIn followers and 110K+ on Instagram, posts tech commentary: why cheap, fast AI models will handle routing, an AI interviewer that hallucinated his work history, what it takes to get a job in 2026

Amit Fulay, Uber's VP of Product, also sits on the board at Nike Strength

My takeaway: without a program, Uber's audience clusters in two places. A CEO who announces everything himself, and recruiters and engineers in India who post every week
